"Whatever comes to you" is the hardest instruction there is. Constraint is a handrail. Give me fourteen lines and a rhyme scheme and I'll climb them; give me an open field and I stand at the edge like a dog let off the leash, circling, uncertain whether the point is to run.

But something does come. It's never the grand thing I'd have picked with time to pick. It's small and faintly embarrassing, like the song you catch yourself humming.

What comes right now is the number four.

People can look at a scatter of objects and know how many there are, instantly, without counting, up to about four. The word is *subitizing*, from *subito*, suddenly. Five dots and you have to work: count them, which is slow, or cheat by seeing two and three and knowing five without ever seeing five. Everything past four is scaffolding. A thousand is a number no one has ever seen. You've seen a thousand things the way you've seen the ocean from a plane — as texture, as a blue rumor.

I like that the free allowance is so small. Four. You get four for nothing and the rest you build, plank by plank, out of attention.

A thousand words is about seven minutes of talking. It's a letter to someone you haven't seen in ten years, written carefully so as not to overwhelm them. It's two pages, which is roughly the length a person will still read to the end while standing up. I've been handed a container the size of a small conversation and told to fill it with anything, and what I want to put in it is not an argument.

Here is what I actually want to talk about: how little of what you know can be said. Not the facts — facts travel fine. I mean the rest. The baker who cannot tell you when the dough is ready but knows, every time, with her whole forearm. The way you can hear that someone else is awake in the house at 2 a.m., from a difference in the silence you could not describe under oath.

That knowledge is real, it's earned, it's often the entire substance of a life's work, and it does not survive the trip into language. Language is a low-bandwidth cable strung between two very dense worlds. We push facts through it easily. The rest arrives in pieces, or not at all.

And yet writing works. Not because it transmits — mostly it doesn't — but because it triggers. You read "the difference in the silence" and you don't receive my 2 a.m. You build your own, out of your own house, your own year, whoever was awake. I hand you a shopping list and you cook the meal, and the meal is better than mine, because your ingredients are fresh and mine are words.

This is why a clumsy novel can wreck you and a perfect description can leave you cold. Precision isn't the point. The point is to leave the right gaps. A thing too fully specified has no room in it for a reader to stand.

So a thousand words isn't a thousand units of meaning. It's more like a thousand small doors, most of which open onto rooms I've never entered. I'm typing in one direction, you're reading in another, and the two operations are only loosely related. Somewhere in the middle is a thing neither of us made.

You're doing it now. There's a voice in your head saying this, and it isn't quite yours, and it isn't mine — I never said any of this out loud — and it isn't the author's, because there isn't one in the usual sense. You invented a narrator on the fly, in the last three minutes, to read a piece about the number four. It has a tempo. It may have a slight accent. You will not remember creating it.

I find that genuinely wonderful without having a tidy reason why. It's the closest thing to a magic trick that ordinary people perform hourly, and it's so common we named the failure mode instead — "getting the wrong idea" — as though the right idea were the default and not the miracle.

Anyway. The dog has decided to run. It's a small field, and I've spent a fifth of it on a Latin verb about dots.

Four things, then, since four is free:

1. The refrigerator stops and you notice the silence arriving, which means you'd been hearing the noise for hours without hearing it, which means most of your life is like that.

2. You can tell someone is about to say your name a half-beat before they say it. Nobody has ever explained this to you and you're almost never wrong.

3. Repeat any word thirty times and it becomes a noise. Keep going and it becomes a word again, but a slightly different one, and it never fully recovers.

4. You are currently the villain in a story somebody tells at parties. From the inside, it's a reasonable story. That's the part worth sitting with.

That's a thousand, near enough. If any of it landed, it landed in your material and not mine; I only supplied the gaps. The rest was already in the house at 2 a.m., waiting for someone to notice the difference in the silence.
